lines: The exact same customer sits inside a sales system under one name and one spelling, and inside a finance system under a slightly different one, each with its own separate key and its own separate credit limit.
Nobody ever decided which of those two records was actually correct.
A report that counts customers simply counts both of them, and that one customer quietly becomes two.
Before I show you how this actually gets fixed, think through this with me.
Does fixing a duplicate like this always require rewriting one of those two original systems directly, replacing whatever it already has on file?
Or is there a way to fix it entirely outside both of those systems, without changing either one of them at all?
answer: Two of the four approaches this lesson covers never write anything back into either original system at all.
Both of them resolve the very same duplicate in a separate layer that sits outside the two systems completely, leaving each one exactly as it already was.

lines: Here's the lightest of these four approaches.
A separate layer simply cross-references the two systems' own keys against each other, without ever copying either system's actual data anywhere else.
Neither original system changes at all. Each one keeps right on being the one true version of its own record.
Here's a second approach that goes one step further than simple cross-referencing.
A separate layer actually gathers both systems' records together and assembles one single, clean copy meant purely for reporting.
That clean copy never gets written back into either original system. Each one keeps being the true version of its own record, exactly like the first approach.
Here's a third approach that behaves quite differently from the first two.
A separate layer still keeps its own single copy, but that copy now actually gets synchronized back into both original systems in both directions.
Both of those original systems stay fully writable on their own, the same as before, but now they're also kept in sync with that shared copy.
Here's the fourth and most demanding of these four approaches.
One single system becomes the only place this kind of record can ever be created or changed at all, full stop.
Every other system that used to write its own version of that record now simply reads from this one system instead of writing anything itself.
The more control that one single system demands over writing, the less freedom every other system keeps to run its own part of the business independently.
Here's how a team actually builds one of those clean, assembled copies in practice.
Records first get standardized into one consistent shape, then matched against each other, then merged using a fixed rule for which source wins each individual field, then finally published.
Whatever that fixed rule genuinely can't decide on its own simply waits in a queue for an actual person to look at and resolve by hand.
Here's why this entire problem actually matters to a real business in the first place.
The exact same customer, the exact same product, or the exact same physical plant can genuinely exist inside two or more completely separate systems at once.
Whichever one of these four approaches a team actually picks decides exactly what kind of agreement those separate systems will have about that one shared thing.
Let's gather what today actually covered, because every piece of it comes back to the exact same two questions.
Simple cross-referencing, an assembled reporting copy, a copy synced in both directions, and one single system that owns everything outright.
Every single one of those four approaches is really just a different answer to who gets to write, and where the one true copy of a record actually lives.
One more question, because picking the right approach here genuinely depends on what a team actually needs.
A company wants every one of its order systems to keep writing its own orders directly, with no brand new single system taking over that job.
But that same company also wants one single, clean, duplicate-free customer list purely for its own reporting. Which of today's four approaches actually fits that company's situation?
answer: The approach that assembles a clean reporting copy fits perfectly here, since it never asks any existing order system to give up writing its own orders.
Taking full ownership away from every other system is exactly the one thing this particular company already ruled out wanting.
